newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh warns investors to avoid kerb market.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh warns investors to avoid kerb market.

text.p: Shares on Dhaka bourse fell on Wednesday after the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) warned investors to avoid the kerb market and steer clear of trading in 24 companies it said were in the red.
"The share prices are falling and there is a tremendous selling pressure in the market. Almost all the issues dipped in early trading," one broker told Reuters by phone from the trading floor.
He said BD Lamps fell 289 taka to 7,700 and Olympic Industries shed 74 taka to 1,740. Most other shares may fall as well, he added. Neither company was included in the SEC warning.
The SEC, the country's market watchdog, issued a notification on Wednesday warning investors of possible risks in trading on rumour or without verifying the economic fundamentals of companies.
"Purchase and sale of securities at places other than the stock exchange is illegal," said the SEC notice, broadcast on television and published by newspapers on Wednesday.
The SEC move followed an unprecedented rise in share prices amid buying by retail investors, who have been encouraged by the country's new-found political stability.

SEC Member Alamgir Kabir said the move was intended to make investors aware of the possible consequences of trading in the fast-growing kerb market -- trading that takes place outside the official market.
"There is likelihood of one being cheated in such a market. It (trading) should be done through stock brokers or dealers," he told Reuters.
He added: "We also don't want to see the investors panicked. We feel it's our responsiblity to make the investors aware of the current situation."
The DSE benchmark index closed at 2,087.38 on Tuesday following two bullish weeks. The index was at 1,649.51 on September 24 and at 1,145.54 on August 1.
The market capitalisation reached $3.44 billion on Tuesday, almost unchanged from Monday's level, but up from $2.0 billion on August 1. It was at $452 million at the end of 1994.

Kabir said the SEC had also indentified 24 listed companies whose price rises were not backed by adequate assets or earnings. SEC officials said 19 of the companies had an accumulated loss of about $40 million. The other five were either liquidated or closed down long ago.
"The investors (are) behaving like wild horses. Believe it or not, a company's 100-taka share traded at 1,971.5 taka ($46)," said one official, referring to one of the 24 companies.
Kabir said the number of retail investors rose to 500,000 from 250,000 three months ago.
He said public interest had increased due to the current political stability and government steps to privatise and boost the stock market.
DSE officials said about 10,000 retail investors were crowding the streets outside the DSE building every day.
They said the recent surge in stock prices was also because of the shortage of good scrips in the market.
